sections.title: The voyage that lost 1,400 men
sections.intro_md:
In 1740 Commodore George Anson left England with six ships and about 1,900 men to raid Spain's Pacific trade. Almost four years later his flagship came home loaded with silver. Roughly 1,400 of his men did not come home, and most of them died of a disease that a handful of lemons a week would have prevented.

The cure was not a secret. English and Portuguese captains had used oranges and lemons more than a century earlier. It was found, written down, ignored, half-adopted, garbled and lost again, over and over, until a Hungarian chemist pulled the missing molecule out of paprika in 1932.

This day follows that loop, and the fruit itself, born in the hills of north-east India and Myanmar.

spotlights.name: Anson's voyage round the world
spotlights.spot_it: A naval squadron that rounded Cape Horn, lost most of its men to sickness and still came home with a Spanish treasure galleon.
spotlights.story_md: Anson's squadron rounded Cape Horn in 1741 into months of storms. By the time the survivors limped to the Juan Fernandez Islands in June, the crews of the three ships still afloat had shrunk from 961 men to 335. Gums swelled over teeth, old wounds reopened, men died in their hammocks. Anson pressed on anyway, crossed the Pacific in the *Centurion* and on 20 June 1743 captured the Manila galleon *Nuestra Senora de Covadonga*, carrying 1,313,843 pieces of eight. Britain cheered the silver. A Scottish naval surgeon named James Lind read the death toll instead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous scurvy disaster in British history, and the book that made Lind start his trial.
spotlights.memory_hook: Silver in the hold, scurvy in the hammocks.

sections.title: What scurvy is, in numbers
sections.intro_md:
Scurvy is what happens when the body runs out of vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid. Most animals make their own. Humans cannot, so every milligram has to come from food.

It is slow. Symptoms appear only after at least a month with little or no vitamin C. First comes tiredness and aching limbs, then bleeding gums, loose teeth, easy bruising, tiny red spots in the skin, and wounds that will not heal. Old fractures can come apart. Untreated, it kills, usually through bleeding or infection.

It is also absurdly easy to fix. About **10 mg a day**, the vitamin C in a few slices of orange, prevents and reverses the disease. Recovery begins within days of treatment and is usually complete in a few weeks. The numbers below explain why sailors on salt meat and biscuit for months were the perfect victims, and why scurvy has never quite disappeared.

spotlights.name: Scorbutic gums
spotlights.spot_it: Swollen, spongy, purple gums that bleed at a touch, sometimes growing over the teeth.
spotlights.story_md: The mouth is where sailors first saw it. Gums turn purple and spongy and can swell until they cover the teeth; a chronicler of Magellan's voyage wrote that some men's gums grew over their teeth so they could not eat, and that nineteen died of it. Teeth loosen because the ligaments holding them are made of collagen, the protein scurvy unpicks. The breath turns foul. Elsewhere the skin roughens and bruises at a knock, tiny red spots called petechiae appear, the hair changes, and bones and muscles ache. Listlessness and low mood often come first, which is one reason ships' surgeons blamed laziness.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The classic sign that tells a doctor to check vitamin C, even today.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the gums swallow the teeth, think C.

spotlights.name: Ascorbic acid, the molecule
spotlights.spot_it: A small ring-shaped sugar acid, six carbons, structurally close to glucose; the white powder sold as vitamin C.
spotlights.story_md: Vitamin C is a modest molecule: six carbon atoms in a ring, built from glucose by most animals in four enzyme steps. Its name records the disease it cures. When Norman Haworth worked out its structure in 1933, he and Albert Szent-Gyorgyi proposed calling it a-scorbic acid, 'against scurvy', from the medieval Latin *scorbuticus*, cognate with Old Norse *skyrbjugr*. It is fragile. Heat, air, light, copper and long storage destroy it, which is the single fact that explains most of the confusion in this story. Cooking can cut the vitamin C in vegetables by around 60%, and pasteurising milk wipes out the little it had.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first vitamin ever made in a laboratory, in 1933.
spotlights.memory_hook: A-scorbic: literally 'anti-scurvy'.

sections.title: Why your body falls apart without it
sections.intro_md:
Collagen is the most common protein in the body. It is the rope in skin, gums, blood vessel walls, tendons, scar tissue and the scaffold of bone. Each collagen molecule is three chains twisted together, and the twist holds only if certain building blocks, proline and lysine, have an extra oxygen and hydrogen bolted on.

The enzymes that bolt them on, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, carry an iron atom that keeps getting knocked out of its working state. Vitamin C hands it an electron and resets it. No vitamin C, no reset, and the body keeps making collagen that cannot hold its shape. Capillaries leak, gums soften, wounds stay open. Vitamin C also helps make carnitine, which muscles need to burn fat, and noradrenaline, which may explain the early fatigue.

The deeper question is why we need to eat it at all. The answer is a broken gene.

spotlights.name: Collagen and the iron reset
spotlights.when: Mechanism worked out in the 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: A triple-twisted protein rope; vitamin C is the helper that lets its enzymes finish every knot.
spotlights.story_md: Hydroxyproline, the modified building block that vitamin C makes possible, is the single most common chemical modification in all human proteins. The enzyme that makes it needs iron in its ferrous state, oxygen and a molecule called alpha-ketoglutarate; vitamin C keeps the iron ready. Without it, new collagen is floppy and weak. Old collagen does not vanish at once, which is why scurvy takes weeks to show, but the body is always replacing it. That is why the first places to fail are the ones that turn over fastest or take the most strain: the gums, the walls of tiny blood vessels, healing wounds and growing bone in children.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns scurvy from a mystery into plumbing: the body loses the ability to make its own glue.
spotlights.memory_hook: No C, no knots in the collagen rope.

spotlights.name: GULO, the gene we broke
spotlights.spot_it: A dead gene, GULOP, still sitting on human chromosome 8, full of mutations.
spotlights.story_md: Most mammals make vitamin C in four steps from glucose. The last step needs an enzyme called L-gulonolactone oxidase, or GULO. In the ancestors of monkeys, apes and humans the gene broke about 63 million years ago, around the time our branch of primates split from the lemurs, which still make their own. A wreck of it, the pseudogene GULOP, remains on chromosome 8. Guinea pigs broke the same gene on their own about 20 million years ago, and several bats did too. Living on fruit made the loss harmless, so nothing selected against it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Explains why a sailor gets scurvy and the ship's rat does not.
spotlights.memory_hook: The rat in the hold made its own vitamin C; the sailor could not.

sections.title: Found, then forgotten: 1497 to 1740
sections.intro_md:
The striking thing about the early history of scurvy is how often the right answer was in someone's hands. Portuguese sailors had citrus trees and vegetable gardens planted on St Helena as a hospital stop. A Spanish friar recommended oranges and lemons in print in 1579. An English captain ran what amounts to a controlled comparison in 1601. The first surgeon of the East India Company told his apprentices to carry lemon juice in 1617. A Dutch-based doctor wrote in 1734 that scurvy was owed 'solely' to the lack of fresh vegetable food.

None of it stuck. Fresh fruit rotted at sea. Learned physicians ashore, who had never seen a scurvy ward, explained the disease through bad air, salt, damp and faulty digestion, and dismissed sailors' cures as anecdote. Historians estimate scurvy killed at least two million sailors between 1500 and 1800. Jonathan Lamb's figures are blunt: Vasco da Gama lost 116 of 170 men in 1499, and Magellan's expedition 208 of 230, mainly to scurvy (other causes are mixed into those totals).

spotlights.name: Vasco da Gama
spotlights.spot_it: The Portuguese captain who opened the sea route to India; portraits show a heavy beard and the cross of the Order of Christ.
spotlights.story_md: On the first European voyage round Africa to India, da Gama's crews fell sick on the East African coast. Historians of vitamin C note that the curative effect of citrus fruit was already known on this expedition. The voyage home was worse. By the time the fleet reached Malindi in January 1499 about half the crew had died and many of the rest had scurvy. There were not enough healthy men to sail three ships, so da Gama had the *Sao Rafael* scuttled. Of roughly 170 who left Lisbon, Jonathan Lamb counts 116 dead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The route to India was paid for in scurvy, and the cure was already in Portuguese hands.
spotlights.memory_hook: Da Gama found the sea road to India and sank a ship he had no men to sail.

spotlights.name: Cartier and the annedda tree
spotlights.spot_it: A French explorer frozen in at Quebec, and an evergreen with flat, scale-like sprays: probably eastern white cedar.
spotlights.story_md: Jacques Cartier's ships froze into the St Lawrence at Stadacona, modern Quebec City, with ice more than a fathom thick. Scurvy broke out, first among the Iroquoians, then the French. By mid-February, he wrote, 'out of 110 that we were, not ten were well enough to help the others'. Domagaya, an Iroquoian man who knew the French, told him of a remedy made from a tree called annedda. The French boiled its bark and needles into a tea, stripped a whole tree in a week, and recovered. The tree was probably eastern white cedar, whose needles were later measured at about 50 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. Cartier repaid the help by kidnapping the chief, Donnacona, when he sailed home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A working cure, taught by Indigenous people in 1536, that Europe failed to carry to sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ask the people who live there: the cure was a cedar tea.

spotlights.name: Lancaster's lemon juice
spotlights.spot_it: An Elizabethan merchant captain; the commander of the first English East India Company fleet.
spotlights.story_md: James Lancaster's four ships left Torbay on 21 April 1601 for the East Indies. Every morning, men on his own ship, the *Red Dragon*, took three spoonfuls of bottled lemon juice. The other three ships did not. By August scurvy had broken out on those three, and when the fleet reached Table Bay on 9 September their crews were so weak that Lancaster's men had to help work them into harbour. He then stopped at Madagascar for more citrus. The Company read his report. The Royal Navy would make lemon juice compulsory only in 1795, nearly two centuries later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A ready-made comparison, one ship against three, 146 years before Lind.
spotlights.memory_hook: One ship took three spoons a day; three ships did not.

spotlights.name: John Woodall and The Surgeon's Mate
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded Jacobean surgeon, and a printed page headed 'Of the Scurvy called in Latine Scorbutum'.
spotlights.story_md: John Woodall was the first Surgeon General of the East India Company and supplied every Company ship's medicine chest. In 1617 he published *The Surgeon's Mate*, a manual for young surgeons sent to sea, and devoted pages 160 to 176 to scurvy. His advice matched what mariners already knew: fresh food if possible, and if not, oranges, lemons, limes and tamarinds, with lemon juice kept in the chest. He could not explain why it worked, and physicians ashore, who believed scurvy was a digestive disorder, took no notice. Note the tamarind: a sour pod familiar to every Indian kitchen, on an English naval surgeon's list.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The cure was printed in English 130 years before Lind's trial.
spotlights.memory_hook: Woodall wrote it down in 1617: lemons, limes and tamarind.

spotlights.name: Fray Agustin Farfan
spotlights.spot_it: A friar-physician in a woodcut portrait, from 16th-century Spain's empire.
spotlights.story_md: Agustin Farfan was a Spanish friar and physician. In 1579 he published a medical book that recommended oranges and lemons for scurvy, a remedy his text says was already known in the Spanish navy. Spain's empire had a structural advantage: dozens of ports where fresh fruit could be bought. Two centuries later the Spanish naval officer Alessandro Malaspina, whose surgeon Pedro Gonzalez swore by oranges and lemons, led an expedition from 1789 to 1794 with almost no scurvy at all. The citrus cure was arguably a Spanish and Portuguese commonplace long before Britain claimed it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that the 'British discovery' was old news in Iberian navies.
spotlights.memory_hook: Spain had the oranges and the ports.

sections.title: James Lind's twelve sailors
sections.intro_md:
On 20 May 1747 the surgeon of HMS *Salisbury*, cruising in the Channel, took twelve men with scurvy and did something unusual: he made them as alike as he could, gave them the same diet and the same quarters, and split them into six pairs, each with a different popular cure. That design, comparing treatments side by side in similar patients at the same time, is the seed of every modern clinical trial.

The result was dramatic. But the rest of the story is less tidy than the legend. Lind's trial filled only a few paragraphs of a long, complicated book. He kept believing scurvy had several causes, including damp air and blocked sweat. He recommended a boiled fruit concentrate that destroyed the very thing that worked. The Navy took 42 more years to act. Historians now read him as a careful observer who ran one brilliant experiment and then got lost in theory.

data.daily_cure: 25 drops of elixir of vitriol (dilute sulphuric acid)

data.result: One fit for duty in six days, the other nearly well

data.daily_cure: Spicy paste of garlic, mustard seed, myrrh and more, with barley water

spotlights.name: The Salisbury trial
spotlights.spot_it: A calm Georgian face in a powdered wig; a title page reading 'A Treatise of the Scurvy, in three parts'.
spotlights.story_md: During a ten-week cruise, 80 of the *Salisbury*'s 350 men went down with scurvy. Lind chose twelve with similar symptoms. The pair given two oranges and a lemon a day ran out of fruit after six days, by which time one was fit for duty and was put to nursing the others. In 1753, now a physician in Edinburgh, Lind published *A Treatise of the Scurvy* and dedicated it to Anson. He also reviewed everything written on scurvy before him, in effect a systematic review. Yet the trial took up a few pages, and the Navy's Sick and Hurt Board rejected a proposal to supply fruit juice the following year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the first controlled clinical trials ever reported, the template for how medicine tests a cure.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve sailors, six pairs, one pair got oranges.

spotlights.name: The rob: how Lind boiled his own cure away
spotlights.spot_it: A thick syrup of lemon or orange juice, evaporated over hours in nearly boiling water and stored in bottles.
spotlights.story_md: Fresh fruit would not keep on long voyages, so Lind proposed a 'rob': juice concentrated by slow evaporation over several hours. It was compact and kept for years. It was also nearly useless, because heat destroys vitamin C. Captain Cook carried rob on his first voyage, and later observers saw no benefit from it, which gave doctors one more reason to doubt citrus. Lind also listed vegetables for preventing scurvy that modern analysis says would have done little. His own data from the Haslar naval hospital, where he saw 1,146 scurvy cases among about 5,740 patients in two years, were never published in numbers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best intentions, the wrong chemistry: a lesson in how a good finding gets diluted.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lind boiled the vitamin out of his own cure.

spotlights.name: Haslar naval hospital
spotlights.spot_it: A long brick hospital on the Gosport shore facing Portsmouth harbour.
spotlights.story_md: In 1758 Lind became chief physician of the Royal Naval Hospital at Haslar, then one of the largest hospitals in the world, with about 1,500 patients on an average day. During the Seven Years' War its wards filled with scorbutic sailors; the Navy lost far more men to disease than to battle. At Haslar he pushed clean clothes, bathing and ventilation, which cut typhus. In 1953 a plaque to him was unveiled at the University of Edinburgh medical school. It was paid for by the citrus growers of California and Arizona.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where Lind spent 25 years, and where his trial became a career.
spotlights.memory_hook: His memorial was paid for by orange growers.

sections.title: How the Navy finally beat it
sections.intro_md:
What changed minds was not a paper. It was captains. Cook came home from long Pacific voyages with healthy crews. Officers who had used lemon juice at Gibraltar and in the Caribbean demanded it. In 1794 Rear Admiral Alan Gardner, about to sail against Mauritius, refused the official remedies of malt, wort and elixir of vitriol and asked for lemons. The expedition was cancelled, but HMS *Suffolk* sailed for India in spring 1794 with lemon juice and sugar aboard.

She reached Madras after a non-stop voyage of 23 weeks with no serious scurvy and a crew healthier than when it left. The daily dose was two-thirds of an ounce of juice in grog, just about the 10 mg that prevents the disease. In June 1795 the Admiralty, pushed by the physician Gilbert Blane and the Sick and Hurt Board, ordered a daily lemon ration for every ship. By 1800 the supply chain worked, and a navy that could blockade France for months gained an advantage historians still argue about.

spotlights.name: Captain Cook and the sauerkraut
spotlights.spot_it: The official portrait of Cook in naval blue, and a bowl of pale shredded fermented cabbage.
spotlights.story_md: Cook's *Endeavour* left in 1768 carrying 7,860 pounds of 'Sour Kroutt', enough for two pounds a week per man. His sailors at first refused it. So Cook had it served every day at the officers' table. 'The moment they see their superiors set a value upon it,' he wrote, 'it becomes the finest stuff in the world.' On the second voyage of 1772 to 1775, over three years at sea, only four of 118 men died, none of scurvy. The irony: Cook credited malt wort, which had almost no vitamin C, while the real work was done by sauerkraut, fresh greens bought at every landfall and strict cleanliness.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a long voyage could be healthy, wrapped in the wrong explanation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Serve it to the officers and the crew will want it.

spotlights.name: Gilbert Blane
spotlights.spot_it: A Georgian physician in a dark coat, portrait by Martin Archer Shee.
spotlights.story_md: Blane was Physician to the Fleet under Admiral Rodney from 1779 to 1783, off Gibraltar and in the West Indies, where he demanded monthly sickness reports from every ship's surgeon and improved the sailors' diet. He pushed lemon juice in print, and in 1795 he joined the Sick and Wounded Board as a commissioner. That year, against the theories of the London medical establishment, the Admiralty adopted lemon juice as a daily addition to every sailor's diet. Where Lind had found the answer and hedged it, Blane was the administrator who turned it into supply contracts, which is where most public health victories are actually won.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The man who turned a finding into a ration.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lind found it; Blane bought it in bulk.

spotlights.name: Alessandro Malaspina
spotlights.spot_it: An officer in Spanish naval uniform, leader of a five-year scientific voyage.
spotlights.story_md: Malaspina's five-year Spanish scientific expedition, from 1789 to 1794, was the first major long-distance voyage that experienced virtually no scurvy. His surgeon, Pedro Gonzalez, was convinced fresh oranges and lemons were essential. The one outbreak came on a 56-day open-sea crossing: five men fell ill, one seriously, and all five were well three days after landing at Guam. Spain's network of ports made fresh fruit easy to buy. In English-language histories the expedition is far less famous than Cook's voyages, though by this measure it did better.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first long exploring voyage with virtually no scurvy was Spanish, not British.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five sick on the open sea, five well three days after Guam.

spotlights.name: Scurvygrass
spotlights.spot_it: A low coastal plant with small white four-petalled flowers and fleshy kidney-shaped leaves.
spotlights.story_md: *Cochlearia officinalis* earned its English name because it worked. Sailors carried it dried in bundles or as distilled extracts. Its leaves are bitter, so cooks hid the taste with herbs and spices, and in Britain scurvygrass drinks and even sandwiches became a fashion that lasted into the 19th century, fading only as citrus became cheap. Lind later suggested growing cress on wet blankets aboard ship.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A folk remedy that was right, preserved in a plant's name.
spotlights.memory_hook: Its name is the instruction label.

sections.title: Limes, limeys and how the cure was lost again
sections.intro_md:
Having won, Britain proceeded to lose. During the Napoleonic Wars Mediterranean lemons became hard to get, and limes from Britain's own Caribbean colonies were cheaper and, people thought, better, because they were sourer. Everyone believed the acid was what mattered. In 1845 ships in the West Indies switched to lime juice, and by 1860 lime juice was used across the Royal Navy. The Merchant Shipping Act of 1867 made a daily 'lime or lemon juice' ration law on merchant ships too, and gave the world the word **limey**.

Limes carry roughly half the vitamin C of lemons. The juice was also pressed, piped through copper and stored in the light for months, all of which destroy what little remained. A 1918 test of Navy and merchant lime juice on animals found it had almost no antiscorbutic power. Steamships made voyages shorter, so for decades nobody noticed. Then expeditions went to the poles, the official juice failed, and doctors concluded citrus had never been the answer.

spotlights.name: Limey and Rose's lime juice
spotlights.spot_it: A slang word for a Briton, and a concentrated lime cordial born of a shipping law.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1850s Royal Navy sailors were mocked as 'lime-juicers', later shortened to 'limey', mostly in North America; the word drifted to mean any British person. In 1867, the year merchant ships were legally required to carry lime or lemon juice, Lauchlin Rose patented a way to preserve citrus juice without alcohol, creating a concentrated drink. Rose's lime juice became nearly ubiquitous at sea, and the bottle outlived its purpose ashore as a sweet cordial. The cruel twist is that the product most associated with beating scurvy was, by then, nearly useless against it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The insult and the cordial are fossils of a public health policy that quietly failed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Limey: named after the fruit that did not work as well.

spotlights.name: The British Arctic Expedition
spotlights.spot_it: A three-masted steam sloop, HMS Alert, locked in pack ice off Ellesmere Island.
spotlights.story_md: HMS *Alert* and *Discovery* tried to reach the North Pole through Smith Sound. *Alert* got to Floeberg Beach at 82 degrees north on the tip of Ellesmere Island, and in spring 1876 man-hauled sledge parties set out to explore and to try for the Pole over the ice. Then scurvy broke out, men died, and the expedition turned back. An inquiry blamed the commander, George Nares, for not sending lime juice on the sledges; it froze solid and was hard to use. Critics pointed out that men on the ships, drinking their lime juice daily, got scurvy too. Both sides were half right, and neither knew why.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A disaster that made the failure of lime juice visible, and was misread.
spotlights.memory_hook: The juice froze, and so did the theory.

spotlights.name: The Belgica, frozen in
spotlights.spot_it: A small three-masted ship anchored below snowy Antarctic peaks.
spotlights.story_md: The Belgian Antarctic Expedition was seriously hit by scurvy because its leader, Adrien de Gerlache, at first discouraged the men from eating penguin and seal meat. That was exactly the wrong call. Uncooked fresh meat, notably liver and other organs, holds enough vitamin C to prevent scurvy and even partly treat it, and even cooked fresh meat keeps some, because cooking rarely heats the whole piece through. The lesson, that fresh meat works, was real, and it fed a new and wrong idea: that the problem was spoiled tinned food, not a missing nutrient.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A polar crew made ill by refusing fresh meat, which confused the citrus story further.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eat the penguins.

spotlights.name: Edward Evans on the Barrier
spotlights.spot_it: A young naval officer in a peaked cap; Scott's second in command on the Terra Nova expedition.
spotlights.story_md: Scott's first Antarctic expedition, in 1902, had cured early scurvy with fresh seal meat. Yet the theory of the day still blamed 'ptomaine poisoning' from tinned meat. On the Terra Nova expedition, Lieutenant Edward Evans led the last support party back from near the Pole in early 1912 and collapsed with scurvy. Tom Crean and William Lashly pulled him on the sledge. When he could go no farther, Crean walked alone for 35 miles in about 18 hours to Hut Point on 18 February and raised help, and Evans survived.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Scurvy was still nearly killing polar explorers five years after the cure was found in guinea pigs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Crean walked 35 miles alone so that Evans would not die of scurvy.

spotlights.name: Vilhjalmur Stefansson and the year of meat
spotlights.spot_it: A Canadian Arctic explorer with a broad face, who lived for years on Inuit food.
spotlights.story_md: Stefansson spent years with Inuit hunters who ate almost no plants and did not get scurvy. To convince sceptics, in February 1928 he and a companion began eating nothing but meat for a year at Bellevue Hospital in New York, under medical observation. They stayed well. Studies of traditional Inuit, Dene and Metis diets later put vitamin C intake at about 52 to 62 mg a day, from raw and lightly cooked meat, organs and fish. The point was never that meat beats fruit. It was that freshness, not the food group, carried the vitamin.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Explains why Arctic peoples never needed lemons.
spotlights.memory_hook: Raw and fresh beats fruit that has sat in a barrel.

sections.title: Finding the molecule, 1907 to 1937
sections.intro_md:
The breakthrough came from a mistake with animals. In 1907 two Norwegian doctors studying beriberi, a different deficiency disease, switched from pigeons to guinea pigs and fed them grain. The guinea pigs got scurvy. Until then scurvy had been thought to be an exclusively human disease, and nobody could test a cure without waiting for sailors to fall ill. Now anyone could.

In 1912 the Polish biochemist Casimir Funk proposed that some diseases are caused by missing 'vital amines', or vitamins, and the antiscorbutic factor became 'water-soluble C'. A race followed. Albert Szent-Gyorgyi isolated a reducing substance from adrenal glands that he called hexuronic acid. Charles Glen King's lab in Pittsburgh, testing extracts on guinea pigs, proved in spring 1932 that this was the vitamin, and published without crediting Szent-Gyorgyi, starting a lasting priority quarrel. Norman Haworth solved and synthesised the structure in 1933, the first vitamin ever made artificially, and Tadeus Reichstein's process made it cheap.

Nobel Prizes to Szent-Gyorgyi (medicine) and Haworth (chemistry)

spotlights.name: Holst and Frolich's guinea pigs
spotlights.spot_it: Two Norwegian doctors, and the small tailless rodent that turned out to share our broken gene.
spotlights.story_md: Axel Holst and Theodor Frolich wanted to study the beriberi that struck Norwegian fishing crews. Pigeons were the usual test animal, but they wanted a mammal, and chose guinea pigs. Fed on grain and bread, the guinea pigs did not get beriberi. They got scurvy, a disease nobody had seen in an animal before. It was luck twice over: pigeons, as seed eaters, make their own vitamin C in the liver and can never get scurvy, while mice and rats make it too. Holst and Frolich then showed which fresh foods prevented it, years before the word vitamin existed. This animal model has been called the single most important piece of vitamin C research.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gave science a way to test antiscorbutics in weeks instead of voyages.
spotlights.memory_hook: They went looking for beriberi and found scurvy in a guinea pig.

spotlights.name: Albert Szent-Gyorgyi and the paprika
spotlights.spot_it: A lean Hungarian scientist with a high forehead; and a pile of red, yellow and green peppers.
spotlights.story_md: Szent-Gyorgyi isolated his hexuronic acid from animal adrenal glands, and ran out. Fruits and vegetables failed as a source. In autumn 1932, in Szeged, the paprika capital of Hungary, he tested paprika peppers. In his own telling, he did not feel like eating the paprika his wife served for supper, took it to the lab instead, and by midnight knew it was 'a treasure chest full of vitamin C'. Within a week his team had made over three pounds of pure crystals. He did not patent it. He sent batches free to researchers, including Haworth, and to the League of Nations to use where scurvy persisted. He won the 1937 Nobel Prize in medicine, and in 1940 handed his Nobel medal to Finland, then at war with the Soviet Union.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Turned vitamin C from a trace into a substance chemists could hold in kilograms.
spotlights.memory_hook: He would not eat his paprika, so he extracted it.

spotlights.name: Norman Haworth
spotlights.spot_it: A sugar chemist; the man whose ring diagrams of sugars are still called Haworth projections.
spotlights.story_md: Haworth was a carbohydrate chemist at the University of Birmingham. Using Szent-Gyorgyi's paprika crystals, he worked out the structure of the vitamin and in 1933 proved it by building it from scratch, the first vitamin made by chemical synthesis. He and Szent-Gyorgyi then proposed the name a-scorbic acid, which stuck as ascorbic acid. Haworth shared the 1937 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Paul Karrer, 'for his investigations on carbohydrates and vitamin C'. In the same year Szent-Gyorgyi won the medicine prize: one molecule, two Nobels in one year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proved the vitamin was a known kind of molecule that a factory could make.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two Nobels, one year, one molecule.

spotlights.name: Tadeus Reichstein's process
spotlights.spot_it: A five-step route from glucose to vitamin C, half chemistry, half bacteria.
spotlights.story_md: At the ETH in Zurich, Tadeus Reichstein and colleagues devised a way to make vitamin C from ordinary glucose in 1933. Glucose is turned into sorbitol, bacteria ferment that into sorbose, and chemistry does the rest. The patent was sold to Hoffmann-La Roche in 1934, which marketed the result as Redoxon. A cheaper two-step fermentation route, developed in China in the 1960s, is now standard. Reichstein later shared a Nobel Prize for work on adrenal hormones. His process is why vitamin C, once the rarest of substances, became the most widely taken dietary supplement in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Made scurvy prevention cost almost nothing.
spotlights.memory_hook: From sugar to vitamin C, with bacteria doing one step.

sections.title: Three wild fruits and the family tree
sections.intro_md:
Now the fruit. A 2018 study in *Nature* sequenced 60 kinds of citrus and found the genus was born in the south-east foothills of the Himalayas: eastern Assam, northern Myanmar and western Yunnan. In the late Miocene, as the monsoons weakened, the ancestor split rapidly into species. Later some crossed the Wallace Line into New Guinea and Australia and became the Australian limes.

The study counted ten natural species. Three matter most for your kitchen: the **citron**, the **pomelo** and the **mandarin**. Almost every commercial citrus, the sweet orange, lemon, lime and grapefruit, is a hybrid of two or more of them, sometimes with a fourth wild species, the micrantha papeda, in the mix. Citrus crosses so easily, and survives so well by grafting, that one lucky seedling can become a world crop. That also makes the naming chaotic: 'lemon', 'lime' and 'orange' are kitchen words, not family names.

visual.title: Who is a child of whom

data.parents: Pomelo x mandarin, a separate cross

spotlights.name: Citron
spotlights.spot_it: A big, lumpy, thick-skinned yellow fruit that is mostly white pith with little juice.
spotlights.story_md: The citron is the oldest citrus in cultivation and the first to reach the Mediterranean. Theophrastus, Aristotle's pupil, described it as the 'Median or Persian apple', with thorns like a wild pear; it was grown in the Middle East long before other citrus, and Alexander's armies are often credited with carrying it west. The fruit does not drop from the tree and can reach 3.6 to 4.5 kg. Its thick white albedo is rich in pectin and vitamin C. It is one of the pure founding species, a parent of the lemon, and its fingered form is Buddha's hand.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The father of the lemon and the first citrus the West ever saw.
spotlights.memory_hook: The citron is all coat and no juice.

spotlights.name: Pomelo
spotlights.spot_it: The giant of the family: a pale green or yellow fruit as big as a head, with a thick soft rind and dry, firm segments.
spotlights.story_md: The pomelo, *Citrus maxima*, is the largest citrus fruit and a natural, non-hybrid species. It gave the sweet orange its mother: the orange's chloroplast DNA, inherited only through the seed parent, is pomelo DNA. Pomelo genes also sweeten the mandarins we eat today; the *Nature* study found that the more pomelo ancestry a mandarin has, the larger and less sour its fruit. It is also an ancestor of the bitter orange and the grapefruit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sweetness in oranges and modern mandarins comes largely from this fruit.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pomelo is the orange's mother.

spotlights.name: Mandarin
spotlights.when: Wild in southern China and nearby
spotlights.spot_it: A small, flattened orange fruit with a thin, loose, easy-peel skin.
spotlights.story_md: The mandarin is the third founding species, and the wild ancestor was bitter. Nearly all commercial mandarins carry pomelo genes that made them sweet. It sits behind tangerines, clementines, satsumas, the Nagpur orange, the Khasi mandarin, the Coorg mandarin and the kinnow. The sweet orange is roughly 58% mandarin by ancestry. The *Nature* paper describes a tangled network of relatedness among mandarins and oranges that records thousands of years of selection by farmers. If an orange peels easily in one spiral, you are probably holding a mandarin.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's most-grown citrus is a mandarin, even when it is sold as an 'orange'.
spotlights.memory_hook: If it peels with your thumb, it is a mandarin.

sections.title: Their children: oranges, lemons, limes and stranger things
sections.intro_md:
Every citrus in the market is a story of crosses and accidents. The grapefruit, for one, is a sweet orange crossed back with its own mother, the pomelo. The sweet orange is a single ancient cross between a hybrid pomelo and a mandarin; every orange variety since, navel and Valencia and blood orange, descends from that one prototype and differs only by mutations farmers noticed and grafted. The bitter orange is a separate, perhaps wild, cross of the same two parents. The lemon is a citron crossed with a bitter orange. Limes are a muddle of citron, mandarin, pomelo and papeda.

How sour they are matters for this story. Lemon juice is about 5 to 6% citric acid, roughly five times the acidity of orange juice. Sourness is not vitamin C, which is why the Navy's 'sourer is better' guess about limes was wrong. The other fruits here, Buddha's hand, the makrut lime and Australia's finger lime, show how far the family has wandered from the fruit bowl.

spotlights.name: Sweet orange
spotlights.when: First mentioned in China in 314 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: A round orange fruit with a tight peel that does not slip off, white star-shaped blossoms and glossy leaves.
spotlights.story_md: The sweet orange arose in domestication somewhere in southern China, north-east India or Myanmar, and the earliest written mention is Chinese, from 314 BCE. It reached the Mediterranean only in the late 15th or early 16th century with Italian and Portuguese merchants, and became a luxury: a few sit on the window sill in van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait, one of their first appearances in Western art, and Versailles finished its great Orangerie in 1686. Spanish settlers took it to Florida in 1565. In 2024 the world grew 67 million tonnes of oranges, and Brazil alone grew 23% of them. One serving, a navel orange, holds about 83 mg of vitamin C.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most planted fruit tree on earth began as a cross in the eastern Himalaya.
spotlights.memory_hook: One ancient cross, every orange since.

spotlights.name: Lemon
spotlights.when: Possibly first millennium BCE, north-east India
spotlights.spot_it: An oval yellow fruit with a nipple at one end, white flowers flushed purple.
spotlights.story_md: A true lemon is a hybrid of citron and bitter orange. Its birthplace is uncertain, but some evidence points to north-east India in the first millennium BCE. The English word travelled the same road as the fruit: from Persian *limun*, a general word for citrus that is cognate with Sanskrit *nimbu*, into Arabic, Italian and French. Its juice is 5 to 6% citric acid. Mediterranean lemons were the fruit that actually kept the Royal Navy healthy from 1795 until the switch to limes. Today India and Mexico lead the world in lemons and limes combined, 23.6 million tonnes in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The fruit that won the scurvy war; its name is a cousin of nimbu.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lemon and nimbu are the same word that took different roads.

spotlights.name: Key lime and Persian lime
spotlights.spot_it: Small, round, seedy and thin-skinned (Key); or bigger, oval and almost seedless (Persian).
spotlights.story_md: 'Lime' is a kitchen word for several unrelated hybrids. The Key lime, the West Indian lime of the Royal Navy, is small, seedy and very sour; historically it spread from South-East Asia. The Persian or Tahiti lime is larger and nearly seedless. Limes have roughly half the vitamin C of lemons. That is why the Royal Navy's switch from Mediterranean lemons to West Indian limes, between 1845 and the 1860s, weakened its scurvy protection just when long Arctic and Antarctic expeditions began. Limes are usually picked green, when flavour and acidity peak; left on the tree, many turn yellow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Navy's 'more acid, more cure' guess, refuted by a lime.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half the C, all of the sour.

spotlights.name: Bitter (Seville) orange
spotlights.spot_it: Rough, deep orange fruit on city street trees, too sour to eat raw: the marmalade orange.
spotlights.story_md: The bitter orange, *Citrus x aurantium*, is a pomelo-mandarin cross distinct from the sweet orange. It reached Sicily in the 9th century, during Arab rule, centuries before the sweet orange. Its raw pulp is not usually eaten, but it is higher in pectin than the sweet orange, giving marmalade a better set. Every winter fruit from Seville's street trees is shipped to Britain for marmalade, though Andalusians rarely eat it. It is also a parent of the lemon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The orange that is never eaten raw, yet runs through Europe's food history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seville's oranges are for jam, not for eating.

spotlights.name: Buddha's hand
spotlights.spot_it: A bright yellow citron split into long curling fingers, with no pulp or juice inside.
spotlights.story_md: Buddha's hand is a citron whose fruit splits into finger-like segments. Inside there is no pulp and no juice, only rind and pith, which can be candied or zested. It is grown mostly for its scent, and in China and Japan it perfumes rooms and clothes. It is given as an offering at Buddhist temples, where tradition prefers fruits whose fingers close together like a hand in prayer. Its origin is traced to north-east India or China, the same cradle as the rest of the family.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof of how strange one citrus species can look.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lemon that grew fingers and forgot the juice.

spotlights.name: Makrut lime
spotlights.spot_it: A small, knobbly green fruit; hourglass leaves that look like two leaves joined end to end.
spotlights.story_md: *Citrus hystrix* is a thorny shrub whose bumpy green fruit, about 4 cm across, has thick skin and little juice. The prize is the leaf: an hourglass shape made of a leaf blade plus a flattened, leaf-like stalk. The rind and crushed leaves give an intense citrus scent used across South-East Asian cooking and in perfume. Its older English name, kaffir lime, is now often avoided because the word is an ethnic slur in South Africa; makrut lime and Thai lime are common alternatives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A citrus used for its leaves more than its fruit.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two leaves in one, and a name in dispute.

spotlights.name: Australian finger lime
spotlights.spot_it: A slim, finger-shaped fruit full of tiny round juice beads, nicknamed citrus caviar.
spotlights.story_md: When citrus spread south-east, some crossed the Wallace Line, the deep-water boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife, into New Guinea and Australia. There they became a separate group, the Australian limes. The finger lime, *Citrus australasica*, is the most striking: cut it open and its juice vesicles spill out as separate, firm little beads. The *Nature* study dates this southern radiation to the early Pliocene; other summaries put it later, in the early Pleistocene. Either way it came millions of years after the first split in the Himalayan foothills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows citrus is an Asia-to-Australia family, not a Mediterranean one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Citrus caviar from across the Wallace Line.

sections.title: How citrus went round the world
sections.intro_md:
Citrus travelled with armies, faiths and merchants. The citron went west first, through Persia; Jewish ritual made it portable, because the festival of Sukkot requires one. Arab rule brought the bitter orange and lemon to Sicily and Spain. Portuguese and Italian traders brought the sweet orange to the Mediterranean around 1500, and Spanish ships carried oranges to the Americas from 1493. Each move left words behind: the orange came into English through French and Italian from Arabic *naranj*, Persian *narang* and Sanskrit *naranga*.

Then came industry. A seedless orange mutant found at a monastery in Bahia, Brazil, made California's fortune. Frozen orange juice concentrate, developed in Florida after the Second World War, turned oranges into a breakfast commodity; by 1949 Florida plants were making over 10 million gallons a year. Today Brazil grows nearly a quarter of the world's oranges and supplies much of its juice.

Nokrek, Garo Hills: Indian wild orange
Riverside, California: the parent navel trees

spotlights.name: The etrog
spotlights.spot_it: A citron, often with a little knob (the pitam) at its tip, held with palm, myrtle and willow at Sukkot.
spotlights.story_md: Leviticus 23:40 asks for the 'fruit of a goodly tree' at the Feast of Tabernacles, and Jewish tradition reads that as the citron, the etrog. Every Sukkot, Jews hold it with the lulav, a palm frond bound with myrtle and willow, and wave them during prayers. Special care goes into choosing one, and varieties whose style stays attached as a little knob, the pitam, are usually preferred. The Hebrew word probably comes from Persian, a trace of the route the citron took west. The ritual demand helped spread citron growing around the Mediterranean.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A religious rule that moved a fruit across continents.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hold it, wave it, do not bruise it.

spotlights.name: The navel orange of Bahia and Riverside
spotlights.spot_it: A seedless orange with a small second fruit, the 'navel', buried at the end opposite the stem.
spotlights.story_md: Early in the 19th century a sweet orange tree at a monastery in Bahia, Brazil, produced a mutant: a fruit with a tiny twin growing inside its end, and no seeds. Seedless means it can only be propagated by cutting and grafting, so every navel orange on earth is, in effect, a piece of that one tree. In the 1870s the US Department of Agriculture imported trees from Brazil, and in 1873 Eliza Tibbets planted two in Riverside, California, where the fruit was sold as the 'Washington' navel. It built the southern California citrus industry, and the University of California later built a Citrus Experiment Station there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One mutant branch, cloned for two centuries, became an industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every navel orange is a clone of one Brazilian tree.

spotlights.name: Orange juice from concentrate
spotlights.spot_it: A glass of opaque orange liquid; once, a small frozen can mixed with water.
spotlights.story_md: During the Second World War American soldiers often threw away the vitamin C-packed lemon drink powder in their K-rations because it tasted bad. The government, the Florida Department of Citrus and a group of scientists set out to make something better than canned juice. Frozen concentrated orange juice arrived three years after the war ended, and by 1949 Florida plants were turning out over 10 million gallons. It was cheap, high in vitamin C and convenient, and it made orange juice a daily breakfast habit. Health advice now often favours whole fruit, since juice carries about as much sugar as some soft drinks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Turned vitamin C into a supermarket commodity.
spotlights.memory_hook: The war that wanted vitamin C gave us breakfast juice.

sections.title: The India connection
sections.intro_md:
India sits at the root of this story. The citrus cradle identified in 2018 includes eastern Assam, and the Garo Hills of Meghalaya still hold wild citrus in a national gene sanctuary. The word orange itself probably began in India: English took it from Arabic *naranj*, Persian *narang* and Sanskrit *naranga*, which may come from a Dravidian word like Tamil *naram*, or, a Lund University linguist suggests, from a Tibeto-Burman language of the north-east such as Garo. Lemon is a cousin of *nimbu*.

Today India, with Mexico, leads the world in lemons and limes, and much of what it calls 'orange' is really mandarin: the Nagpur orange, the kinnow of Punjab and Haryana, the Khasi mandarin of the north-east and the Coorg mandarin of Kodagu. Four names, one species.

Yet deficiency is common. A 2011 study of more than 5,600 people aged 60 and over found vitamin C deficiency in **73.9%** in north India and **45.7%** in south India, more often in men, tobacco users and households cooking on wood or dung fires.

spotlights.name: Memang narang, the Indian wild orange
spotlights.spot_it: A small wild citrus of the Garo Hills, *Citrus indica*, protected in Nokrek's National Citrus Gene Sanctuary.
spotlights.story_md: Nokrek, at 1,418 metres the highest point of the Garo Hills in Meghalaya, holds a rare cluster of wild citrus. After Indian wild oranges, *Citrus indica*, were found there in 1984, part of the Nokrek biosphere reserve was declared the National Citrus Gene Sanctuary. The Garo call the fruit memang narang and use it for jaundice and stomach complaints, and in spiritual practice. It was long thought the most 'primitive' citrus, perhaps the ancestor of all; genome work shows it is a hybrid with a citron mother and mandarin and papeda in the mix. It is endangered, threatened by slash-and-burn clearing, and confirmed wild only in Meghalaya, close to where the 2018 study placed the birthplace of all citrus.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's own wild citrus, kept as insurance for the world's orchards.
spotlights.memory_hook: Narang in the Garo Hills, naranj in Arabic, orange in English.

spotlights.name: Nagpur orange
spotlights.spot_it: A loose-skinned, bright orange mandarin, often green-patched, piled high on Vidarbha carts in winter.
spotlights.story_md: The 'orange' that made Nagpur India's Orange City is botanically a mandarin, *Citrus reticulata*. It received a Geographical Indication tag in 2014, so only fruit from the region can use the name. It has two seasons: the **Ambiya** crop reaches markets in October and the **Mrig** crop between February and March. Scientists say other mandarins are often passed off as Nagpur oranges outside Vidarbha. The fruit peels easily, as a mandarin should, and is juicy and sweet-sour. In October 2026 growers reported drought had cut Ambiya yields by 30 to 50% in places and shrunk the fruit from the standard 70 mm girth to about 60 mm.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's best-known citrus, and a GI product under climate stress.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nagpur's orange is really a mandarin.

spotlights.name: Kinnow
spotlights.spot_it: A smooth, glossy, deep orange mandarin, seedy and very juicy, sold by the crate across north India in winter.
spotlights.story_md: The kinnow is a Californian. Howard B. Frost crossed the King and Willowleaf mandarins at the University of California Citrus Experiment Station in Riverside around 1915, and the variety was named and released in 1935. It stayed a minor crop in California and Arizona, about 900 acres in 1964, but in the Punjab it found a home. It is now the most widely planted mandarin in Pakistan, and in India it is grown across Punjab and neighbouring Haryana, where Sirsa district grows over half the state's crop. In 2026 'Sirsa Kinnow' became Haryana's first farm product with a GI tag of its own: GI No. 1101, its certificate sealed in Chennai on 28 March 2026 and announced in July.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A fruit bred in California that became the taste of a north Indian winter.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Riverside, raised in Punjab.

spotlights.name: Mosambi juice
spotlights.when: Name from Mozambique, via the Portuguese
spotlights.spot_it: Pale green-yellow sweet limes, low in acid, squeezed into thin, mild juice at roadside stalls.
spotlights.story_md: The mosambi, or sweet lime, *Citrus limetta*, is a citron and bitter orange cross with so little acid that it tastes almost bland. The South Asian varieties trace back to Mozambique, carried by the Portuguese, and the name mosambi records that route; in Tamil Nadu and Kerala it is sathukudi. As a vitamin C source it is decent, not exceptional, and best squeezed fresh: juice that stands for hours, or is heated, loses much of its vitamin. Indian farm statistics often count mosambi with sweet oranges, so the name covers more than one fruit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday citrus drink of India, named after an African coast.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mosambi: Mozambique in a glass.

spotlights.name: Amla, the Indian gooseberry
spotlights.spot_it: Hard, pale green, six-lobed round fruits on feathery branches; mouth-puckeringly sour and astringent.
spotlights.story_md: Amla, *Phyllanthus emblica*, is not a citrus at all, but it often beats one. Measurements across cultivars range from about 193 to 720 mg of vitamin C per 100 g of fresh fruit, against about 53 for an orange or a lemon. Its tannins make it bitter and astringent, and it is a staple of Ayurveda. Hard and long-keeping, it is pickled, candied as murabba and dried, a cheap year-round source many Indian households already have.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's own vitamin C champion, older than any orange in the subcontinent's kitchens.
spotlights.memory_hook: One amla can out-C several oranges.

spotlights.name: Scurvy at the siege of Kut
spotlights.spot_it: A British-Indian division besieged in a bend of the Tigris; the general who surrendered it, beside his Ottoman captor.
spotlights.story_md: In the siege of Kut in Mesopotamia, General Townshend's 6th Division, most of it Indian, ran short of food. In late January 1916 rations were halved, and on 28 January the first horsemeat was issued. Indian soldiers refused it. Hindu, Muslim and Sikh soldiers alike feared being shunned at home: no village would give them daughters to marry. They were given extra atta instead, and the hospital filled with sepoys sick with scurvy. A British inquiry noted that Indians who had eaten horseflesh were less affected. On 12 April officers were ordered to eat it or lose rank, and the men followed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Scurvy in the 20th century, in an Indian army, shaped by caste and food rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: No horsemeat, no fresh food, and scurvy filled the wards at Kut.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Lind discovered that citrus cures scurvy.** Fact: sailors and surgeons had known it since at least 1601, and Lind himself hedged it.

**Myth: oranges are the best source of vitamin C.** Fact: weight for weight, amla, guava, red peppers, kiwifruit and even broccoli beat them. A navel orange is a good source, not the top one.

**Myth: limeys were saved by limes.** Fact: lemons did the saving; the switch to limes weakened protection.

**Myth: big doses of vitamin C prevent colds.** Fact: in the general population, regular vitamin C does not reduce how often people catch colds. It shortens them slightly, and it does seem to halve the risk in people under extreme physical stress.

**Myth: scurvy is extinct.** Fact: cases have risen in rich countries, especially among children with very restricted diets.

**Myth: more is always better.** Fact: the body saturates. Blood levels plateau once intake passes about 1,250 mg a day, and above 3,000 mg diarrhoea is common, which is why the US upper limit is 2,000 mg.

visual.title: Vitamin C, mg per 100 g of raw food

spotlights.name: Linus Pauling's megadoses
spotlights.spot_it: A double Nobel laureate, photographed in the 1940s, who later took grams of vitamin C a day.
spotlights.story_md: Pauling won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the 1962 Peace Prize. In 1966 the chemist Irwin Stone persuaded him that humans, having lost the GULO gene, needed far more vitamin C than official advice. Pauling took 3 grams a day and in 1970 published *Vitamin C and the Common Cold*, a bestseller. He argued for at least 2,300 mg a day and later claimed that 10 grams a day could help late-stage cancer. A 2013 Cochrane review of 29 trial comparisons with 11,306 people found regular vitamin C did not cut how often ordinary people catch colds, and shortened colds by about 8% in adults. The cancer claims remain unproven.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous case of a great scientist being wrong outside his field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two Nobels, three grams a day, no fewer colds.

spotlights.name: The real vitamin C champions
spotlights.spot_it: Guava, acerola cherries and Australia's Kakadu plum: three fruits that leave oranges far behind.
spotlights.story_md: Weight for weight, the orange is a middling source: about 53 mg per 100 g, the same as a lemon. Guava has about 228, amla about 445 in one widely used table, acerola from Brazil about 1,677, and Australia's Kakadu plum, *Terminalia ferdinandiana*, between 1,000 and 5,300. Red peppers beat it too, which is why Szent-Gyorgyi could pull kilograms of pure vitamin from Szeged paprika. Raw matters: cooking can destroy around 60% of the vitamin C in vegetables, and leaching into cooking water takes more. For daily needs, five servings of varied fruit and vegetables give about 150 to 200 mg, ten to twenty times the scurvy threshold.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Puts citrus in its place: famous, useful, not exceptional.
spotlights.memory_hook: Guava beats orange; raw beats cooked.

sections.title: Scurvy has not gone away
sections.intro_md:
Scurvy is now rare, but not rare enough. It turns up in refugee camps, where rates of 5 to 45% have been reported, in famine, and after war: there were outbreaks in Afghanistan in 2002. In rich countries it finds people who eat a very narrow diet: older people living alone, people with alcohol dependence, people who have had weight-loss surgery, and children who eat only a handful of foods.

In the United States, a national analysis of 19.4 million children's hospital stays found scurvy rose from 8.2 per 100,000 in 2016 to 26.7 per 100,000 in 2020. About two-thirds of the children in that analysis also had an autism diagnosis; many such children eat only a handful of foods, such as rice, pasta or crackers. US national survey data for 2017 to 2018 found 6.8% of adults deficient in vitamin C, with smokers at about double the risk.

It is easy to miss: the first signs are leg pain, limping, tiredness and bruising, and in children the X-ray picture can mimic rickets, bone infection or brittle bone disease. A blood test and vitamin C settle it, with improvement in days.

visual.title: US children in hospital with scurvy, per 100,000 stays

spotlights.name: The new scurvy patients
spotlights.spot_it: A child who will not walk because the legs hurt; an adult with bruises and bleeding gums after weight-loss surgery.
spotlights.story_md: Modern cases look different from the sailors'. In 2024 doctors at Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital in Perth described a man in his early 50s with a painful rash and bruising. He had had bariatric surgery, ate poorly, took acid-suppressing drugs and had a low income; his vitamin C was undetectable. Daily vitamin C cleared it. The authors warned that rising food costs and more weight-loss surgery, and perhaps the new weight-loss drugs, could create a 'perfect storm'. In children, orthopaedic surgeons now flag scurvy as a cause of unexplained leg pain and limping, and X-rays of bones can show its tell-tale changes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A disease of explorers has become a disease of diets that are too narrow.
spotlights.memory_hook: If the diet has no fruit or vegetables at all, think of the sailors.

spotlights.name: The Brisbane coroner's findings
spotlights.spot_it: A Queensland coroner's written findings on a six-year-old boy's death.
spotlights.story_md: Queensland's deputy state coroner, Stephanie Gallagher, published findings in late August 2026, without an inquest, on the death of six-year-old Connor Dean. He had Down syndrome and had become a very fussy eater. Admitted to Queensland Children's Hospital in July 2024 with weeks of leg pain and limping, he had a cardiac arrest after a general anaesthetic for an MRI and died on 10 August 2024. His vitamin C was below 1 micromole per litre against a normal range of 20 to 120, and scans showed bone changes of scurvy. His multivitamin listed no vitamin C. The coroner accepted that the deficiency was the most likely underlying factor, and published the findings to warn others.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A reminder that missing scurvy can still kill, in a modern hospital, in 2024.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leg pain plus a very narrow diet: test for vitamin C.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The fruit is in more trouble than the disease. Citrus greening, or huanglongbing, is a bacterial infection spread by a tiny sap-sucking insect, the Asian citrus psyllid. Infected trees yellow, drop fruit and die, and there is no cure. It reached Florida in 2005.

**Florida.** The state grew 244 million boxes of oranges in 1997-98. The USDA's season summary for 2025-26, published on 27 August 2026, put the crop at 12.95 million boxes, about 5% of that peak, though up 5% on the year before. On 9 October 2026 the first forecast for 2026-27, cut by the freezes of early 2026, was 10 million boxes, down another 23%.

**Brazil**, the world's orange-juice giant, finished 2025-26 at 292.94 million boxes. In September 2025 greening affected nearly 48% of orange trees in its main citrus belt. On 8 May 2026 Fundecitrus forecast 255.2 million boxes for 2026-27, down 12.9%, blaming fewer fruits per tree, more fruit drop and greening. A wet winter raised that to 263.15 million in September.

**India.** On 23 October 2026 Nagpur growers reported drought losses of 30 to 50% in parts of the Ambiya crop. In July 2026 Haryana announced the GI tag for Sirsa's kinnow.

spotlights.name: Citrus greening and its psyllid
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny mottled brown insect on a young citrus leaf; trees with yellowing veins and blotchy leaves.
spotlights.story_md: Farmers in Chaozhou, in southern China, were talking about a 'yellow dragon' disease of citrus by the 1870s, for the yellowing veins it causes; that is the meaning of huanglongbing. It was formally described in 1919. The cause is a *Liberibacter* bacterium, carried from tree to tree by the Asian citrus psyllid, a bug 2 to 3 mm long, or in Africa by a related psyllid. Leaves mottle and fall, roots decay, fruit drops early, and the tree dies. It has hit China, India, Brazil, Mexico and Florida. Growers fight the insect, replant, and hope for resistant trees; in July 2026 a trade report said the USDA had authorised the first HLB-resistant orange variety for planting.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest threat to the world's oranges, and to orange juice prices.
spotlights.memory_hook: A yellow dragon carried by a bug the size of a grain of rice.

spotlights.name: The orange juice squeeze
spotlights.spot_it: Shrinking Florida groves and a Brazilian crop that keeps being revised down.
spotlights.story_md: For decades a glass of orange juice was among the cheapest ways to get vitamin C. Florida's collapse, from 244 million boxes of oranges in 1997-98 to under 13 million, means the state that invented frozen concentrate now matters little to world supply. Brazil's crop decides prices. Fundecitrus forecast 314.6 million boxes for 2025-26 in May 2025, then cut it to 292.94 million as greening and drought bit, and in May 2026 expected 255.2 million for 2026-27, nearly 15% below its ten-year average, before a September revision to 263.15 million. The fruit that conquered scurvy now needs a rescue of its own: resistant rootstocks, insect control and new hybrids, all products of the same crossing that made the orange.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Why the price of your juice is a story about a bacterium.
spotlights.memory_hook: Florida once grew 244 million boxes; now it grows about 13.

sections.title: The best facts
sections.intro_md: The facts most worth repeating at dinner, each checked against a source listed for this day and linked back to the spotlight where the detail lives. Start with these three: the plaque to James Lind paid for by orange growers; the ship's rat that made its own vitamin C while the sailors died; and the 'limey' named after the fruit that worked less well.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
**The disease.** Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency. Without vitamin C, the enzymes that finish collagen stall, so gums, skin, blood vessels and bone weaken. About 10 mg a day prevents it. Humans cannot make vitamin C because our GULO gene broke about 63 million years ago.

**The history.** The cure was found and lost many times: Cartier's cedar tea in 1536, Lancaster's lemon juice in 1601, Woodall's book in 1617, Lind's twelve sailors in 1747. The Royal Navy issued lemon juice in 1795, then switched to weaker limes and lost the cure again. Guinea pigs (1907), Szent-Gyorgyi's paprika (1932) and Haworth's synthesis (1933) finally pinned it down.

**The fruit.** Citrus was born in the foothills where Assam, Myanmar and Yunnan meet. Citron, pomelo and mandarin are the parents of almost everything else. India grows mandarins above all: Nagpur, kinnow, Khasi, Coorg.

**Now.** Scurvy is rising among children with narrow diets, and citrus greening is gutting orange groves in Florida and Brazil.

cards.front: This voyage of 1740 to 1744 lost about 1,400 of 1,900 men, mostly to scurvy. Whose?
cards.back: Commodore George Anson's voyage round the world. He still captured a Spanish treasure galleon in 1743.

cards.front: What disease do these gums show?
cards.back: Scurvy: swollen, spongy gums that bleed, from lack of vitamin C.

cards.front: As little as ___ mg of vitamin C a day prevents and reverses scurvy.
cards.back: 10 mg.

cards.front: How long without vitamin C before scurvy symptoms appear?
cards.back: At least a month; usually one to three months.

cards.front: Why does vitamin C deficiency make gums bleed and wounds reopen?
cards.back: The enzymes that finish collagen (prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase) need vitamin C to keep their iron working. Without it, collagen is weak, so capillaries, gums and scars fail.

cards.front: Why can a rat make its own vitamin C but a human cannot?
cards.back: Humans, apes, monkeys and tarsiers carry a broken GULO gene, disabled about 63 million years ago. Rats still have a working one.

cards.front: Which animal, by luck, gave scientists a scurvy model in 1907?
cards.back: The guinea pig. Like us, it cannot make vitamin C.

cards.front: Which primates can still make their own vitamin C?
cards.back: Lemurs and lorises (strepsirrhines). Monkeys, apes and humans cannot.

cards.front: In 1535 to 1536 his men were saved by a tree tea taught by the St Lawrence Iroquoians. Who?
cards.back: Jacques Cartier, at Stadacona (Quebec). The tree, annedda, was probably eastern white cedar.

cards.front: In 1601, how did James Lancaster's ship stay healthy when three others got scurvy?
cards.back: Every morning his men on the Red Dragon took three spoonfuls of bottled lemon juice.

cards.front: John Woodall's 1617 book The ___ told East India Company surgeons to use lemon juice.
cards.back: The Surgeon's Mate.

cards.front: Who ran the twelve-sailor scurvy trial of 1747?
cards.back: James Lind, surgeon of HMS Salisbury.

cards.front: In Lind's trial, which pair recovered fastest?
cards.back: The pair given two oranges and a lemon a day. One was fit for duty in six days.

cards.front: Why did Lind's 'rob' fail as a scurvy remedy?
cards.back: He concentrated fruit juice by heating it for hours. Heat destroys vitamin C.

cards.front: Who paid for the 1953 Edinburgh plaque to James Lind?
cards.back: The citrus growers of California and Arizona.

cards.front: This captain got his crew to eat sauerkraut by serving it at the officers' table. Who?
cards.back: James Cook, on the Endeavour, 1768 to 1771.

cards.front: The Royal Navy ordered a daily lemon juice ration for every ship in ___.
cards.back: 1795, after HMS Suffolk reached India scurvy-free.

cards.front: Which physician pushed the Admiralty to adopt lemon juice in 1795?
cards.back: Gilbert Blane, commissioner of the Sick and Wounded Board.

cards.front: Name this coastal plant, carried dried on ships against scurvy.
cards.back: Scurvygrass, Cochlearia officinalis.

cards.front: Why did the Navy's switch from lemons to limes bring scurvy back?
cards.back: West Indian limes have about half the vitamin C of lemons, and the juice was further degraded by air, light, copper pipes and storage.

cards.front: What does this bottle explain about the word 'limey'?
cards.back: Rose's lime juice (patented 1867). Lime juice rations gave British sailors the nickname lime-juicers, then limeys.

cards.front: This ship's sledge parties were crippled by scurvy in 1876. Name the expedition.
cards.back: The British Arctic Expedition under George Nares (HMS Alert).

cards.front: Who walked 35 miles alone in 1912 to save Edward Evans from scurvy?
cards.back: Tom Crean, on Scott's Terra Nova expedition.

cards.front: Which Hungarian scientist got vitamin C in bulk from paprika in 1932?
cards.back: Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, at Szeged. Nobel Prize in medicine, 1937.

cards.front: What does the name 'ascorbic acid' mean?
cards.back: 'Against scurvy' (a-scorbic), proposed by Haworth and Szent-Gyorgyi in 1933.

cards.front: Who first synthesised vitamin C, in 1933?
cards.back: Norman Haworth, Birmingham. Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1937.

cards.front: Where did citrus originate, according to the 2018 Nature genome study?
cards.back: The south-east foothills of the Himalayas: eastern Assam, northern Myanmar, western Yunnan.

cards.front: Name the three ancestral species behind most commercial citrus.
cards.back: Citron, pomelo and mandarin.

cards.front: Name this oldest cultivated citrus, the parent of the lemon.
cards.back: Citron (Citrus medica).

cards.front: The largest citrus fruit and the sweet orange's mother. Name it.
cards.back: Pomelo (Citrus maxima).

cards.front: The sweet orange is a cross of pomelo and ___.
cards.back: Mandarin (about 42% pomelo, 58% mandarin).

cards.front: A true lemon is a hybrid of citron and ___.
cards.back: Bitter (Seville) orange.

cards.front: Name this fingered fruit with no juice inside.
cards.back: Buddha's hand, a variety of citron.

cards.front: This knobbly fruit grows on a tree with hourglass-shaped double leaves. Which citrus?
cards.back: Makrut (kaffir) lime, Citrus hystrix.

cards.front: What is the fruit inside these pearls, nicknamed citrus caviar?
cards.back: Australian finger lime, Citrus australasica.

cards.front: This tree in Riverside, California, is the parent of which famous fruit?
cards.back: The Washington navel orange, a seedless mutant from Bahia, Brazil, planted in 1873.

cards.front: Which festival needs this citron?
cards.back: Sukkot. It is the etrog, one of the four species.

cards.front: Trace the word 'orange' back as far as it goes.
cards.back: English from French and Italian, from Arabic naranj, Persian narang, Sanskrit naranga; possibly Dravidian (Tamil naram) or a north-east Indian language such as Garo.

cards.front: Botanically, what is the 'Nagpur orange'?
cards.back: A mandarin (Citrus reticulata). GI-tagged in 2014.

cards.front: This mandarin was bred in California in 1915 and now rules Punjab's citrus. Name it.
cards.back: Kinnow (King x Willowleaf), released in 1935. Sirsa Kinnow was registered as a GI in 2026.

cards.front: Which Indian fruit, not a citrus, can carry several times the vitamin C of an orange?
cards.back: Amla (Indian gooseberry): about 193 to 720 mg per 100 g across cultivars.

cards.front: Where is India's National Citrus Gene Sanctuary?
cards.back: Nokrek, in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya, home of the Indian wild orange (memang narang).

cards.front: Where does the name of this sweet lime come from?
cards.back: Mosambi, from Mozambique, via Portuguese traders.

cards.front: Why did Indian soldiers at Kut in 1916 get scurvy?
cards.back: Food ran short and many refused horsemeat, fearing being shunned at home; without fresh meat or vegetables, scurvy filled the hospital.

cards.front: What did the 2013 Cochrane review find about vitamin C and colds?
cards.back: No fewer colds in ordinary people; colds about 8% shorter in adults; risk halved under extreme physical stress.

cards.front: Which of these two holds more vitamin C, weight for weight?
cards.back: Guava (left), about 228 mg per 100 g, against about 53 for an orange (right).

cards.front: How did US child scurvy hospital rates change from 2016 to 2020?
cards.back: From 8.2 to 26.7 per 100,000 stays, roughly tripling.

cards.front: This 2 to 3 mm insect spreads which citrus disease?
cards.back: The Asian citrus psyllid spreads citrus greening (huanglongbing).

cards.front: What made Lind's 1747 experiment a controlled trial and not just an observation?
cards.back: He picked patients with similar illness, kept diet and quarters the same, and compared several treatments side by side at the same time.

cards.front: What was the weak point of Lind's trial, by modern standards?
cards.back: Only two patients per treatment, no random allocation, and the fruit ran out after six days; he later diluted his own finding with theory.

cards.front: Which picture shows the fruit that actually kept the Navy healthy from 1795?
cards.back: Left: the Mediterranean lemon. Right: the West Indian lime, about half the vitamin C.

cards.front: Where was Florida's citrus collapse measured, and how big?
cards.back: Florida: 244 million boxes of oranges in 1997-98, 12.95 million in 2025-26, and a 10 million box forecast for 2026-27 (October 2026).
