best_facts.fact: The Royal Navy beat scurvy with lemons in 1795, then swapped to West Indian limes with about half the vitamin C, and scurvy came back on polar expeditions.
best_facts.why_surprising: A solved problem was un-solved by a procurement decision.

best_facts.fact: The plaque honouring James Lind, unveiled at Edinburgh's medical school in 1953, was paid for by the citrus growers of California and Arizona.
best_facts.why_surprising: The orange industry funded the memorial to its best advertisement.

best_facts.fact: In 1601, 146 years before Lind's trial, James Lancaster gave one ship of four three spoonfuls of lemon juice a day; its crew had to help sail the other three, sick with scurvy, into Table Bay.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'first' trial had a working precedent.

best_facts.fact: Lind boiled fruit juice for hours to make a portable 'rob', which destroyed the vitamin C that made his oranges work.
best_facts.why_surprising: The discoverer sabotaged his own cure.

best_facts.fact: Humans, apes and monkeys cannot make vitamin C because the GULO gene broke about 63 million years ago; its dead remains still sit on human chromosome 8.
best_facts.why_surprising: We carry the corpse of the gene that would have saved the sailors.

best_facts.fact: Szent-Gyorgyi tested Szeged paprika for vitamin C in autumn 1932 (in his telling, because he did not want to eat it at supper); within a week his lab had made over three pounds of the pure vitamin.
best_facts.why_surprising: A dinner he avoided led to a Nobel Prize.

best_facts.fact: Citrus evolved in the foothills where Assam, Myanmar and Yunnan meet, and the word 'orange' may trace back to an Indian language, through Sanskrit naranga.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'Mediterranean' fruit and its name both come from north-east India's neighbourhood.

best_facts.fact: 'Limey' comes from the lime juice ration, the version of the cure that worked worst.
best_facts.why_surprising: The nickname honours the wrong fruit.

best_facts.fact: Guinea pigs became the scurvy test animal by accident in 1907: Norwegian doctors studying beriberi chose them over pigeons, which make their own vitamin C and could never have got scurvy.
best_facts.why_surprising: A lucky choice of lab animal unlocked the vitamin.

best_facts.fact: Cook got his crew to eat sauerkraut by serving it only at the officers' table; 'the moment they see their superiors set a value upon it, it becomes the finest stuff in the world'.
Every navel orange is a clone of one mutant branch from a monastery tree in Bahia, Brazil; one of the 1873 parent trees still stands in Riverside, California.
best_facts.why_surprising: Billions of oranges, one original tree.

best_facts.fact: The kinnow that defines a Punjabi winter was bred in Riverside, California, around 1915.
best_facts.why_surprising: A north Indian favourite is a Californian immigrant.

best_facts.fact: Florida grew 244 million boxes of oranges in 1997-98 and about 13 million in 2025-26, after citrus greening arrived in 2005.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 95% collapse in the home of frozen orange juice.

best_facts.fact: Hospital scurvy among US children rose from 8.2 to 26.7 per 100,000 stays between 2016 and 2020.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sailors' disease, tripling in the 21st century.

best_facts.fact: Vitamin C won two Nobel Prizes in the same year, 1937: medicine for Szent-Gyorgyi and chemistry for Haworth.
Amla can carry 193 to 720 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, several times an orange.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's sourest berry beats the famous citrus.

best_facts.fact: In WWII American soldiers threw away the lemon drink powder in their rations, which pushed Florida to develop frozen orange juice concentrate.
best_facts.why_surprising: Breakfast juice was a military taste problem.

side_dish.title: Why Lind's twelve sailors still matter: the control group
side_dish.body_md:
Give a sick sailor oranges and he recovers. Did the oranges work? Maybe he would have recovered anyway. One success proves almost nothing.

Lind's trick in 1747 was to make the comparison do the work. He chose twelve men with similar scurvy, gave them the same diet, the same quarters and the same time, and changed only one thing per pair. If everything else is equal and one pair gets better, the difference is probably the treatment. That is a **controlled comparison**, and the group that does not get the treatment you care about is the **control group**.

Modern trials add three more ideas Lind did not have. **Randomisation**: let chance, not the doctor, decide who gets what, so the doctor cannot unconsciously give the fruit to the strongest men. **Blinding**: where possible, neither patient nor assessor knows who got what. **Size**: two people per treatment can mislead; hundreds or thousands give stable answers. The 2013 Cochrane review of vitamin C and colds pooled 29 comparisons and 11,306 people, which is why its answer is more trustworthy than any single study.

The lesson of the scurvy story is also humbling. Lind's comparison was right, and his theory was wrong; the Navy trusted theory. When an experiment and an explanation disagree, back the experiment.

offline_task.title: Watch heat destroy vitamin C, like Lind's rob
offline_task.body_md:
**Twenty minutes, kitchen materials. Do not drink any of the test liquids.**

**You need**
- 1 teaspoon cornflour (or rice starch) and a cup of water
- Tincture of iodine or povidone-iodine antiseptic (the brown liquid in a first-aid kit)
- 2 lemons or 3 nimbu, a small pan, a dropper or teaspoon, 3 clear glasses

**Steps**
1. Boil the cornflour in the water for a minute and let it cool. This is your starch indicator.
2. Put 3 tablespoons of water and 1 teaspoon of starch solution in each glass. Add iodine a drop at a time until each turns the same deep blue-black.
3. Squeeze the lemons. Keep half the juice fresh. Boil the other half for 10 minutes, the way Lind made his rob, then cool it.
4. Add fresh juice to glass 1, one drop at a time, swirling, and count the drops until the blue disappears. Vitamin C turns iodine colourless.
5. Do the same with the boiled juice in glass 2. Use glass 3 to test bottled lemon juice or juice left out overnight.

**What to notice**: the fewer drops it takes to clear the blue, the more vitamin C the juice holds. Boiled and old juice usually need many more drops. You have just repeated, in miniature, the mistake that cost the Navy decades.

Watch the BASF Science Club demonstration first if you want to see the colour change.
